newsitem.title: USA: Judge upholds plan to issue Seattle stadium bonds.
newsitem.headline: Judge upholds plan to issue Seattle stadium bonds.

text.p: A Washington state judge Tuesday upheld a county plan to issue $336 million in municipal bonds to fund a new retractable-roof stadium for the Seattle Mariners baseball team.

In an 11-page decision, Superior Court Judge J. Kathleen Learned said the county's decision to authorize the sale of bonds was legal, rejecting arguments of a taxpayers' group that said it violated the state constitution.

A spokesman for the taxpayers' group said it planned to appeal the ruling. The group, Citizens For More Important Things, also is trying to block the stadium project by forcing a countywide vote before the bonds can be issued.

Chris Van Dyk, coordinator of the group, said the county's plan to charge the Mariners $700,000 annual rent when play begins in 1999 was "absurd" and amounted to an improper gift of public funds to a private entity.
"The interest alone is going to cost $20 million a year," he said. "It would be like charging $150 rent on a $200,000 house."
But Learned said $700,000 cannot be considered a "nominal" amount, and she noted that any profits generated by the stadium must be shared with the county.

"If the bargain struck was not a 'good' one, it is still a constitutional one," Learned said. "The constitution does not exist to protect the public from the weakness or failings of its public officials."

Van Dyk said his group has collected more than 63,000 petition signatures, far more than the 48,000 needed to get the stadium issue on a county ballot by September, which he said would effectively delay issuance of the bonds.

County voters previously narrowly defeated a proposed tax to pay for a new baseball stadium to replace the 21-year-old Kingdome, but in 1995 the state Legislature approved a special county sales taxes and other measures to fund the project and keep the Mariners from leaving Seattle.
Groundbreaking for the new stadium is scheduled to take place March 8.
